 Concerts expose Gen Z spending stereotypes in Vietnam
 Sold-out Hanoi shows reignite debate over young people's spending habits, financial pressures and the right to enjoy life
 Tens of thousands of fans gathered at My Dinh National Stadium in Vietnam's capital to see G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, three members of the popular South Korean band BIGBANG, on Oct. 24 and 25. (Photo: X )
 By Alex Hoang 
 Published: November 04, 2026 10:51 AM GMT 
 Updated: November 04, 2026 10:54 AM GMT 
 --> 
 Share 
 Add as a preferred source on Google 
 Tickets for BIGBANG's two concerts in Hanoi sold out just over an hour after general sales opened in August, despite prices that were high relative to average Vietnamese incomes.
 On Oct. 24 and 25, tens of thousands of fans gathered at My Dinh National Stadium in Vietnam's capital to see G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, three members of the popular South Korean boy band.
 Ticket prices ranged from 1 million to 10.5 million dong (US$38-$400). By comparison, Vietnam's average monthly worker income was about 9.1 million dong during the first nine months of 2026, according to the national statistics agency.
 The most expensive ticket therefore cost more than an average worker's monthly income.
 The concerts were a major success, but they also revived a familiar question on Vietnamese social media: Why do young people complain about low salaries, rising living costs and unaffordable housing, yet spend millions of dong to watch their idols perform for a few hours?

 Some critics linked the spending to Generation Z, often portrayed online as struggling financially while rejecting traditional expectations of hard work and career success.
 Others questioned whether concertgoers should save money or support their parents instead.
 It was not the first such debate. When BLACKPINK, another South Korean group, performed in Hanoi in 2023, tickets costing up to 9.8 million dong sparked similar criticism.
 Three years later, the artists had changed, but the arguments remained much the same.
 A concert full of stereotypes 
 The first problem with the debate is a simple assumption: those buying expensive tickets must be the same young people complaining about financial difficulties.
 But there is little evidence to support that connection.
 A sold-out stadium shows strong demand for one event. It does not prove that millions of young Vietnamese are financially comfortable.
 There is another problem: many BIGBANG fans are not even Gen Z.
 BIGBANG debuted in 2006, while Super Junior, another popular Korean boy band, debuted in 2005. Teenagers who followed these groups nearly two decades ago are now in their 30s or 40s.
 Many have established careers, families, and their own incomes.
 Jamie Nguyen, 33, founder of IELTS Ms. Tra My, an English-language education business in Ho Chi Minh City, flew to Hanoi with friends to attend the concert.
 "I don't really care because they're talking about Gen Z, and I'm well past that age," she said with a laugh.
 "I think everyone has their own way of living and enjoying life. Every football season, tickets costing tens of millions of dong are also sold at this very stadium, but no one cares."
 Her experience highlights something often overlooked: fans grow older alongside their favorite artists.
 Yet online discussions often treat K-pop fandom as an activity for financially dependent teenagers.
 Psychologists call one possible explanation “confirmation bias,” the tendency to notice information that supports existing beliefs.
 Someone who already believes Gen Z spends irresponsibly may see expensive concert tickets as proof, while ignoring older fans or young people who cannot afford to attend.
 The price of personal enjoyment 
 Critics also question what else fans could buy with the same money: a holiday, a new phone, or savings for the future.
 Some commentators suggest that traditional arts or classical music would be a better use of the money than K-pop concerts.
 Comparing different spending choices is reasonable. But such arguments become a distraction when they ignore whether the individual buyer can actually afford the expense.
 After all, money spent on holidays could also be saved, while money spent on new phones could be given to parents.
 Almost any personal pleasure can be criticized if someone insists there is always a better use for the money.
 What makes a concert worth its price may be different for every fan. For someone who grew up listening to BIGBANG, the experience may carry memories that cannot easily be measured in money.
 Why online arguments spread 
 Le Quang Linh, a finance lecturer who also provides psychological counseling to students at a university in Hanoi, said he was surprised that such personal choices could cause so much controversy.
 "A few personal expenses for interests such as music, celebrities or football can hardly tell us anything about a person's financial situation, personal life or character," he said.
 Linh believes many such online arguments are intended to provoke reactions rather than encourage meaningful discussion.
 "I find these online debates rather pointless. I believe they are mainly designed to stir up controversy and attract engagement, rather than contribute anything constructive," he said.
 He added that he regularly advises students to avoid getting involved in meaningless online battles.
 His comments point to a wider question about how social media works.
 A headline such as "Gen Z complains about being poor but spends millions on concerts" creates an immediate conflict.
 Those who agree criticize young people's spending habits. Those who disagree defend their freedom to enjoy their earnings.
 Both sides generate comments, shares and attention.
 Research on online behavior has found that moral outrage can be encouraged by social rewards such as likes and shares. Engagement-based algorithms can also give greater visibility to emotional or divisive content.
 This does not mean every critical post is deliberately written to attract views. Financial pressures and different attitudes toward spending are genuine concerns.
 But blaming an entire generation is easier than examining the circumstances of individual concertgoers.
 A debate beyond Vietnam 
 Similar arguments have appeared abroad. Taylor Swift's Eras Tour sparked debates about ticket prices in the United States, Britain and Australia, while South Korean fans have raised concerns about rising K-pop concert costs.
 In Vietnam, where saving money and supporting parents remain important family expectations, debates over entertainment spending can also become judgments about responsibility and morality.
 What makes the Vietnamese discussion particularly revealing is how quickly questions about ticket prices can turn into accusations about an entire generation's character.
 After BIGBANG's Hanoi shows, fans returned to their jobs, families and everyday responsibilities.

 Many were teenagers when the group first became famous. Today, they can afford to see their childhood idols with money they have earned themselves.
 The online controversy will eventually move to another event. But the habit of judging an entire generation from a few images may continue.
 A sold-out stadium cannot represent the financial situation of millions of people.
 And an expensive evening of entertainment reveals very little about someone's responsibility, character or financial future.
